why: Manufacturing growth captures real-sector economic momentum; sharp contractions precede recession events and fuel social unrest via job losses and industrial hollowing. It complements GDP-level signals with a sector-specific pace measure that responds faster to external shocks and trade disruptions.
coverage_note: WB WDI; broad coverage but thin for small/fragile states and some MENA; data gaps common pre-1980 for lower-income countries.

trends.reason: Manufacturing contraction is a leading indicator of recession; likely to crack the greedy top-40 for this Trend and enter top features.
Positive manufacturing growth is a canonical recovery signal; model should capture the directional swing from contraction to expansion.
Industrial contraction correlates with layoffs and labor unrest; plausibly cracks top-40 in countries where manufacturing is a large sector.
Policy interventions often follow or precede manufacturing trend reversals; medium signal strength in economies with active industrial strategy.
Prolonged manufacturing decline deepens inequality but the relationship is indirect and lagged; marginal lift expected.

why: Private credit depth captures financial leverage and the degree of banking system intermediation; rapid credit expansions are among the strongest known predictors of banking and currency crises, while prolonged contraction signals deflationary stress. The series directly captures the financial-system amplification channel central to economic-stress Trends.
coverage_note: WB WDI; one of the broadest financial series; minor gaps for conflict-affected and sanctioned states in early decades.

trends.reason: Credit booms and busts are textbook banking-crisis predictors; this series directly captures the pre-crisis leverage build-up and is very likely a top-40 entry.
Excessive private credit fuels capital-flow vulnerabilities and FX pressures that culminate in currency crises; consistently appears in crisis literature.
Credit-cycle downturns amplify recessions; negative credit growth flags contraction risk, though recession has many concurrent drivers.
Liberalization events are often accompanied by financial deepening and credit expansion; plausible top-40 entrant for this Trend.
Post-crisis credit collapse forces emergency fiscal responses; tangential upstream signal with indirect causal path.

why: Directly measures the degree to which social media is used to coordinate real-world political violence, capturing a digital mobilization pathway absent from traditional indicators. Provides a near-contemporaneous signal of violence organization that can precede or accompany attacks, political violence events, and protest escalation.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage but v2sm* social media items are only meaningful post-2000; reliable signal from ~2010 onward as social media penetration expanded globally.

trends.reason: Direct mechanistic link: social media coordination of offline violence is definitionally captured by this indicator — very likely top-40 entry for political violence Trend.
Social media mobilization underpins modern protest waves; overlaps substantially with organizing for collective action and protest escalation.
Online radicalization and coordination precede attacks; plausible top-40 entry, though not all terrorism is organized via mainstream social platforms.
Hate speech and incitement on social media fuel communal violence; captures the enabling digital environment for inter-group conflict.
Governments often respond to online-coordinated violence with repression; causal direction may weaken the signal but it is a plausible co-variate.

why: Counts distinct active state-based conflict dyads per country-year, capturing multi-front war complexity that single binary active/inactive flags miss. A country fighting three simultaneous armed groups faces qualitatively different instability than one with a contained single insurgency, making this a unique structural signal.
coverage_note: UCDP; covers all states globally but non-zero values only for ~60-80 conflict-affected countries per year; zero-inflated distribution; complete coverage for active-conflict countries.

trends.reason: Count of active conflict dyads is a core measure of insurgency complexity and directly aligns with the civil war Trend's movement shape; near-certain top-40 entry.
Multiple concurrent state-based conflicts amplify overall political violence and reflect broader state-society breakdown.
Multiple simultaneous conflicts compound displacement, food insecurity, and civilian harm; plausible top-40 entry.
Complex multi-party conflict environments attract foreign intervention as external actors back different warring factions.
High conflict counts create demand for peace processes; the link is real but indirect and temporally delayed.

why: Binary flag for state-based conflict reaching war threshold (≥1,000 battle deaths), distinguishing low-level armed conflict from full-scale war. This threshold crossing historically correlates with regime change, mass displacement, and external intervention events — marking the qualitative escalation that reshapes political trajectories.
coverage_note: UCDP/PRIO-ACD; same coverage as SB conflict series; binary variable so zero-inflated; all active-conflict countries captured with consistent threshold coding.

trends.reason: War-intensity threshold is the definitional ceiling of civil war severity; highest prior for top-40 entry in this Trend.
Interstate wars almost always cross the war threshold; binary flag will be near-perfectly predictive for active war years.
War-level violence drives mass displacement and refugee flows; plausible top-40 entrant for migration/refugee Trends.
War-intensity conflicts historically attract foreign military involvement, either to support a side or impose a ceasefire.
Full-scale war raises military salience and can trigger coups, but causation is contested and the signal is weaker than direct political indicators.

why: Military expenditure as share of GDP is a broad defence-burden and conflict-orientation signal; rapid increases precede militarization events and reflect threat perception, while high sustained levels constrain fiscal space for social spending. SIPRI data is the international gold standard for cross-national military expenditure comparisons.
coverage_note: SIPRI via OWID; comprehensive for most countries from 1988; pre-1988 thinner especially for post-Soviet states and sub-Saharan Africa; small and closed-regime states occasionally missing.

trends.reason: High military spending relative to GDP correlates with oversized armed forces and coup-prone civil-military relations; well-documented in coup literature.
Spending trajectories directly proxy military policy posture; near-certain top-40 entry for this Trend as large shifts accompany structural reforms or demobilization.
Military build-up as share of GDP is a classic arms-race and conflict-preparation signal preceding interstate war.
High military spending combined with aggressive posture often triggers international sanctions; plausible top-40 entry.
Military spending rises during civil wars but also during peaceful deterrence; weaker discriminative signal than conflict-specific indicators.

why: The SDG 2.c.1 Indicator of Food Price Anomalies (IFPA) directly measures domestic food price volatility anomalies, flagging periods when prices diverge sharply from international benchmarks — historically a trigger for mass protests and political instability in food-import-dependent countries. As a real-time early-warning index it is action-oriented rather than purely descriptive.
coverage_note: FAOSTAT SDG 2.c.1; coverage limited to countries with sufficient price series data; shorter time series (~2010+) constrains recipe training on early history; benchmark-year or sparse collection in some countries.

trends.reason: Food price spikes are a canonical mass-protest trigger (Arab Spring 2011, bread-riot literature); IFPA anomaly flag likely top-40 entry for protest Trend.
Domestic food price anomalies co-occur with supply shocks from drought; strong mechanistic link to famine-related event onset.
Food price volatility amplifies humanitarian crises; plausible top-40 entry especially in fragile-state contexts.
Price anomalies disproportionately harm low-income households, worsening inequality and deepening poverty; moderate link to crisis events.
Food price shocks can contribute to broader economic stress but causal direction is often reversed (recession causes food insecurity); marginal lift.

why: Measures whether foreign governments run disinformation campaigns targeting the domestic population, capturing information-warfare interference as a distinct channel of foreign meddling separate from military or economic pressure. Rising scores signal externally manufactured political instability particularly relevant to hybrid-warfare and election-interference scenarios.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage but reliable only post-2000 for v2sm* items; expert-survey based so may lag fast-moving information environments by 1-2 years; pre-2008 values near-zero for most countries.

trends.reason: Foreign disinformation campaigns are a primary tool of hybrid warfare and typically co-occur with or precede other forms of foreign intervention; direct mechanistic alignment.
Election interference via disinformation is the most documented use case; high scores predict contested or delegitimized electoral outcomes.
Exposed foreign disinformation operations frequently trigger diplomatic expulsions and ruptures between targeted and perpetrating states.
Governments targeted by foreign disinformation often respond with increased domestic surveillance and repression to counter perceived foreign-backed opposition.
Foreign disinformation frequently amplifies inter-ethnic grievances; marginal contribution where ethnic fault lines already exist.

why: End-year stock of refugees originating from each country is a cumulative, internationally-validated measure of how dangerous conditions have become for that country's population — effectively a global consensus judgment on origin-country risk. Stocks respond to conflict onset, political repression, and humanitarian crises and persist as slow-moving structural signals.
coverage_note: UNHCR; near-universal coverage; pre-1990 series sparse for many countries; consistent annual data broadly available from ~1990 onward; near-zero values for stable countries still present in series.

trends.reason: REF_COO is the primary refugee stock measure; definitionally aligned with migration/refugee Trend — near-certain top-40 entry.
Mass refugee production is a hallmark of civil war; refugee stock levels strongly co-vary with civil war duration and intensity.
Refugee stock is a core humanitarian crisis metric reflecting cumulative displacement pressure; likely top-40 entry for this Trend.
Refugee flows from non-conflict states are often driven by political persecution; plausible top-40 entry for repression Trend.
Large refugee stocks signal systematic human rights failures in origin country; moderate lift expected.

why: Freedom of peaceful assembly is a direct civil-liberties indicator measuring whether citizens can freely gather for protests and political meetings; restrictions on assembly are an early-stage precursor to mass protest escalation and a marker of political repression that often precedes broader human rights deterioration.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage from 1900; expert-survey methodology provides consistent coding across regime types; high confidence for post-1990 data across all regions.

trends.reason: Assembly restrictions are both a direct antecedent and co-occurring feature of protest events; very likely top-40 entry with strong directional signal.
Banning or restricting assemblies is a canonical repression tool; near-certain top-40 entry for political repression Trend.
Assembly freedom is a core human rights dimension; plausible top-40 entry as part of a civil liberties indicator cluster.
Democratization events are associated with expanding assembly rights; indicator likely captures both the run-up and consolidation phases of transitions.
Assembly rights affect workers' ability to strike and organize collectively; marginal lift as labor action has more direct predictors.
